Regression with brms

Source: vignettes/bison_brms.Rmd
bison_brms.Rmd

bison_brm() fits regression models with the brms package in which a network variable, such as an edge weight, a node metric or a global metric, is the response or a predictor. The uncertainty in the network is included in the results.

bison_brm() takes a number of posterior draws from the edge model (each draw is one possible network that is consistent with the data). It calculates the network variable for each draw, fits the brms model to each resulting dataset and combines the results. This is similar to multiple imputation, a method for missing data in which a model is fitted to several plausible versions of a dataset and the results are pooled. It takes the same arguments as brms::brm(), as well as the edge model(s) and data, and returns a brmsfit object.

Formula syntax

Network variables are specified with bison() in the formula. Inside bison(), give the metric name (see vignette("network_metrics")) followed by the column(s) in the data that identify the dyad, node or network for each row:

Standard formula bison_brm() formula Row of the data frame is a…
edge_weight ~ x bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ x dyad
y ~ edge_weight y ~ bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) dyad
strength ~ x bison(node_strength(node_id)) ~ x node
y ~ strength y ~ bison(node_strength(node_id)) node
degree ~ x bison(node_degree[0.2](node_id)) ~ x node
cv ~ x bison(global_cv(bison_network)) ~ x network

When a list of edge models is given, bison_brm() adds a factor bison_network to the data, giving the position of each edge model in the list. It can be used like any other variable, for example to compare networks or as a random effect.

Some notes:

  • Scale of edge weights. In bison_brm(), edge weights are on the link scale: log-odds (logit) for binary models and log rates for count models. Node and global metrics are calculated from edge weights on the natural scale.
  • Scaling. scale = "z" converts the network variable to z-scores within each posterior draw (subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation), and scale = "centre" only subtracts the mean. Standardising can make priors easier to set. For edge and node metrics, scaling is done separately within each network. This removes differences in the average level between networks, so use scale = "none" to compare levels between networks. For global metrics, scaling is done across networks.
  • Selecting rows. subset selects rows of the data with a logical expression, e.g. subset = sex == "F". Network metrics are still calculated from the whole network.
  • Number of draws. num_draws sets the number of posterior draws used. A model is fitted to each, so more draws take longer. We suggest at least 100 for final analyses.
  • R-hat warnings. R-hat is a convergence diagnostic that compares the MCMC chains (independent runs of the sampler). Because the results of separate models are combined, brms may warn about high R-hat values. This is expected, and convergence of the individual models can be checked with fit$rhats.

Dyadic regression 

library(bisonR)

sim_data <- simulate_bison_model("binary", aggregated = TRUE)
df_edge <- sim_data$df_sim
fit_edge <- bison_model(
  (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1_id, node_2_id),
  data = df_edge,
  model_type = "binary",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary")
)

Edge weight as the response

Edges that share a node are not independent. A multi-membership random effect, (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)), accounts for this by estimating an effect for each node that applies to every dyad the node is part of. It should usually be included in dyadic regressions. bison_brm() gives a warning if it is missing.

fit_dyadic <- bison_brm(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ age_diff + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge
)
summary(fit_dyadic)

Edge weight as a predictor 

bison_brm(
  outcome ~ bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge
)

Comparing edge weights across networks

Give a list of edge models and a matching list of data frames. bison_network identifies the network of each row:

bison_brm(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ bison_network + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  list(fit_edge_control, fit_edge_treatment),
  list(df_edge_control, df_edge_treatment)
)

Nodal regression

The data frame has one row per node, with a column containing the node names used in the edge model:

df_nodal <- data.frame(
  node = levels(df_edge$node_1_id),
  trait = rnorm(10)
)

Node metric as a predictor 

bison_brm(
  trait ~ bison(node_eigen(node)),
  fit_edge,
  df_nodal
)

Node metric as the response 

bison_brm(
  bison(node_strength(node)) ~ trait,
  fit_edge,
  df_nodal
)

Controlling for the network across several networks 

bison_brm(
  bison(node_eigen(node)) ~ trait + (1 | bison_network),
  list(fit_edge_1, fit_edge_2),
  list(df_nodal_1, df_nodal_2)
)

Global regression

Global metrics need a list of edge models, one per network. The data can be a list of one-row data frames, or a single data frame with one row per edge model in the same order:

df_global <- data.frame(
  bison_network = factor(1:2),
  condition = c("before", "after")
)
bison_brm(
  bison(global_cv(bison_network)) ~ condition,
  list(fit_edge_before, fit_edge_after),
  df_global
)

Each network contributes one observation to a global regression, so with only a few networks the results should be interpreted with care.

Priors

Priors describe which parameter values are plausible before the data are seen. bison_brm_get_prior() returns the default brms priors for a model as a brmsprior object, which can be modified in the usual way:

prior <- bison_brm_get_prior(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ age_diff + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge
)
prior$prior[1] <- "normal(0, 1)" # Prior on all population-level effects

bison_brm(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ age_diff + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge,
  prior = prior
)

More

Other brms features, such as different response families or smooth terms, can also be used with bison_brm(). See the brms documentation for details.
